preserved_selected_master_keys_and_speec.raw: If you were sure something would happen, seeing it happen tells you nothing. <bookmark mark='a'/> u after q: no news. <bookmark mark='b'/> A coin landing heads tells you a little. <bookmark mark='c'/> A letter e, a bit more. <bookmark mark='d'/> And a z, which turns up about once in 1,900 symbols, tells you a lot. The less likely it was, the more you learn.

preserved_selected_master_keys_and_speec.raw: Let's turn that into mathematics. Call the surprise of an event with probability p, s of p. <bookmark mark='a'/> Ask a few modest things. It depends only on p. <bookmark mark='b'/> It goes down as p goes up, and a certain event is no surprise at all. <bookmark mark='c'/> For independent events, where one tells you nothing about the other, probabilities multiply and surprises should add: <bookmark mark='d'/> heads on a coin and a five on a die, together, as surprising as the two added up. <bookmark mark='e'/> And small changes in p make small changes in s.

For independent events, where one tells you nothing about the other, probabilities multiply and surprises should add: heads on a coin and a five on a die, together, as surprising as the two added up. And small changes in p make small changes in s.

preserved_selected_master_keys_and_speec.raw: Remarkably, those rules leave only one choice. Measure probabilities in halvings: <bookmark mark='a'/> write p as two to the minus x, and let g of x be its surprise. <bookmark mark='b'/> Rule three says g turns sums into sums. <bookmark mark='c'/> So g of n is n times g of one, for every whole number, <bookmark mark='d'/> and for every fraction. <bookmark mark='e'/> Continuity fills in the rest: g of x is x times g of one.

Let a fair coin flip carry exactly one, and call it a bit: an event of probability p carries log, base two, of one over p, bits.
